text: Declare sensor support per device class (ambient-light auto-brightness, lid and tablet-mode switches, accelerometer rotation) as in or out of scope for 1.0.
Provide a firmware update service (fwupd-class) whose updates are recorded as system-history events.
Audit every linux-firmware blob and vendor firmware used on target hardware for redistribution terms and define a firmware policy of ship, download-on-demand, or exclude per blob.
rationale: Several firmware files are non-redistributable and shipping them in an image is infringement.

text: Define a vendor NDA policy so hardware documentation under NDA can inform but never be reproduced in open-source drivers.
rationale: Target-hardware enablement will involve NDA material that must not taint the codebase.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Ship a user-runnable hardware conformance tool that executes the compatibility suite on an arbitrary machine and submits anonymised, consented results to the compatibility database.
rationale: A public alpha will meet hardware the lab never will and the project needs structured reports instead of forum threads.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide how out-of-tree proprietary kernel modules (notably NVIDIA) are handled under Secure Boot: local machine-owner key signing, vendor-signed builds, or unsupported until an open driver suffices.
rationale: §56.1 names NVIDIA as a hard requirement and Secure Boot makes unsigned proprietary modules unloadable.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Require IOMMU to be enabled and all DMA-capable devices placed behind it on target hardware, with Thunderbolt/USB4 device authorisation (bolt-style) before PCIe tunnelling is allowed.
rationale: Ownership-transfer and DMA-suitable MemoryObjects (§17) are unsafe against malicious peripherals without hardware DMA protection.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Include Secure Boot custom-key enrolment, TPM 2.0 presence and IOMMU support as hardware-selection criteria for the reference AMD desktop, Intel laptop and AMD laptop.
rationale: §62 constrains target hardware but not by security features, and a reference machine that cannot enrol keys cannot exercise the boot security path.

text: Keyboard layout model that reuses xkeyboard-config data, supports layout switching, compose and dead keys, per-window versus global layout policy, and a layout switcher in the shell.
rationale: Non-US keyboard users need layouts from day one of dogfooding and XKB data is mature and must not be reinvented.

text: ADR on printing architecture: IPP Everywhere / driverless-first native print service with PDF as the spool format, CUPS confined to the Linux personality for legacy drivers, and a print job modelled as a typed Operation.
rationale: Printing is a top support burden on every desktop and the baseline never mentions it.

text: OS-owned print dialog and printer discovery (mDNS/DNS-SD, USB, WSD) that grants Capability<PrintJob> for a single job the same way the file chooser grants file authority.
rationale: Apps must not receive ambient printer enumeration or spooler access, so the dialog must be a system authority like the file chooser.

text: Scanning service supporting driverless eSCL/WSD and SANE backends, exposing Capability<Scanner> via a system scan dialog, with a first-party document scanner app.
rationale: Home and office users expect scan-to-PDF to work and it shares discovery and authority design with printing.

text: ADR choosing the PDF rendering and generation library (pdfium, poppler, or a Rust renderer) shared by print-to-PDF, print preview, the document viewer, and the file browser thumbnails.
rationale: PDF is the interchange format for printing and documents and one shared sandboxed renderer avoids four copies of the same attack surface.

text: Bridge compat printing: expose the native print service as a CUPS-compatible IPP socket for Linux apps and as the Wine print spooler for Windows apps.
rationale: Compat applications must print to the same printers with the same dialog to satisfy §49.

text: ADR on the Bluetooth stack: retain BlueZ as an in-kernel/host pair or move the host stack to a userspace native component per §33, with required profiles A2DP, HFP, HID, LE Audio/LC3, GATT and BLE privacy.
rationale: Bluetooth is the classic userspace-driver candidate and §62 requires it to work on laptops with no design stated.

text: Bluetooth pairing agent and device chooser in the shell that grant apps Capability<BluetoothDevice> per paired device, never adapter-wide scanning authority.
rationale: BLE scanning is a location-tracking vector and pairing UI is unavoidable for headphones, mice and keyboards.

text: Thermal and frequency policy daemon (thermald/power-profiles-daemon equivalents) plus laptop function keys, keyboard backlight, and display brightness control exposed as typed settings.
rationale: Without thermal policy the selected laptops throttle or overheat, and hotkeys are the first hardware check reviewers make.

text: Integrate firmware and microcode updates (LVFS/fwupd-style) into system history so firmware changes are recorded, and rollback limits are explicit.
rationale: Firmware is the one update the generation model cannot roll back and users must be told so.

text: Define the hardware compatibility database schema: PCI/USB/DMI identifiers, per-generation status, known issues, workarounds and provenance of each entry.
rationale: The baseline names the database but not what it records or how entries are trusted.

text: Define hardware support tiers (tested in lab, community reported, unsupported) and the criteria for promoting a device between tiers.
rationale: Constrained target hardware needs a public vocabulary so users know what 'supported' means.

text: Support IPP Everywhere/AirPrint network printers, SMB-shared Windows printers and driverless scanning (eSCL) discovered via mDNS.
rationale: Printing is the classic adoption-killer for alternative desktops and mixed-OS households share printers.

text: Support MTP/PTP and local phone-to-desktop transfer for Android and iOS devices.
rationale: Photo import from phones is a top-five desktop task and the first thing a switched user tries.

text: Support fwupd/LVFS-compatible firmware updates for UEFI, SSDs, docks and peripherals.
rationale: Users must not need to boot Windows to update firmware, and reference laptops ship firmware fixes through LVFS.

text: Publish a tiered known-good hardware list (reference, supported, community-reported) with component-level guidance on GPUs, Wi-Fi chipsets, fingerprint readers and docks, regenerated from the hardware compatibility database each release.
rationale: Users buying a machine for JakeOS need a purchase answer, and the constrained target hardware policy in §62 must be communicated.

text: Decide vendor priorities for purchase guidance (AMD graphics first, Intel and MediaTek Wi-Fi, NVIDIA and Broadcom as best-effort) and state them publicly.
rationale: Honest vendor guidance prevents a wave of unsupported-hardware bug reports at public alpha.

text: Ship a pre-purchase and pre-install compatibility checker that inventories PCI, USB, ACPI and firmware identifiers from the live image or from a Windows/Linux host and reports against the compatibility database.
rationale: Users must know before wiping a disk whether their machine works, and the checker doubles as the database's data source.

text: Hardware and compatibility report submissions are opt-in, pseudonymous, reviewable by the user before upload, and contain no serial numbers or network identifiers.
rationale: The compatibility database depends on user telemetry, which is only acceptable to the target audience if it is transparent.

text: Decide the policy for third-party user-space drivers and firmware delivered as signed packages, including review, revocation and how they appear in the compatibility database.
rationale: Vendors and community porters must have a channel to add hardware support without forking the OS.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide whether an IOMMU is a hard hardware requirement for user-space drivers and DMA-capable MemoryObjects, and what degradation applies on systems without one.
rationale: Without IOMMU protection a user-space driver can DMA over the kernel, undermining the entire isolation story.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Prototype a user-space driver for one USB class and one Bluetooth controller (VFIO or native device capability) and measure interrupt latency and throughput against the in-kernel driver.
rationale: The user-space driver strategy is a stated direction but its performance cost is unknown for the classes proposed.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the target hardware list for V1 through V2 (specific AMD desktop, Intel laptop, AMD laptop models) as an ADR before hardware-dependent spikes begin.
rationale: GPU, driver, energy and latency spikes all produce hardware-specific numbers and need a fixed reference set.

text: The initial supported platform is x86-64 desktop and laptop hardware only; no other architecture is a 1.0 requirement.
Retain Linux PCIe support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux USB support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux ACPI support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux power management in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux Bluetooth support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux input device support in the forked kernel.
Retain the thousands of inherited Linux hardware drivers; no fork change may regress a driver without an explicit decision.
Preserve Linux hardware discovery (bus enumeration, device model) unchanged in the fork.
Preserve Linux PCI subsystem in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux USB subsystem in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux ACPI subsystem in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux input subsystem in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux Bluetooth subsystem in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux hardware discovery in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux firmware loading in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux power management in the fork initially.
Define Object<Camera>.
Define Object<Device>.
The Bluetooth service must be restartable with paired devices reconnecting (cross-ref HW).
The printing service must be restartable with queued jobs preserved (cross-ref HW).
Device-management services must be restartable with device capabilities re-issued to holders.
Drivers must live outside the kernel as user-space Components where the performance cost is acceptable.
Build a user-space driver framework providing Object<Device> capabilities, interrupt delivery as Operation completions, and DMA-capable MemoryObjects.
Evaluate and, where acceptable, implement Bluetooth host stack as a user-space driver component.
Evaluate and, where acceptable, implement selected USB device classes as user-space drivers.
Evaluate and, where acceptable, implement sensor drivers as user-space components.
Implement printer drivers as user-space components.
Evaluate remaining peripheral classes (input, cameras, storage bridges) for user-space driver residency.

Document the kernel-residency decision criteria for each driver class: latency requirements, DMA safety, interrupt performance, hardware architecture constraints, and compatibility with inherited Linux drivers.
Do not pursue microkernel purity; drivers may remain in the kernel where the criteria justify it.
Decide the mechanism for user-space driver hardware access: reuse VFIO/UIO-style interfaces, or design a native Device capability with IOMMU-protected DMA via MemoryObject.
Prototype one user-space driver (e.g. a USB HID or USB audio device) and measure latency and throughput against the in-kernel Linux driver.
User-space driver crashes must be isolated: the driver Component restarts under supervision and device capabilities are re-issued (cross-ref §32).
Drivers are recognised as the largest practical blocker; when native-platform work conflicts with keeping Linux hardware support working, hardware support wins.
Long-term driver model supporting three coexisting classes: inherited Linux drivers, userspace native drivers, and selected rewritten in-kernel drivers.
ADR: criteria for classifying each driver as inherited-Linux, userspace-native, or rewritten (latency, DMA safety, interrupt performance, failure isolation value, maintenance cost).
Driver transition must be incremental per device class; no flag-day replacement of any driver class is permitted.
Userspace native driver framework exposing Capability<Device>, interrupt delivery as Operations, and DMA-safe MemoryObjects (cross-ref §33).
Demonstrate at least one inherited Linux driver class (e.g. a USB peripheral class or Bluetooth) migrated to a userspace native driver with measured performance parity.
Driver status registry documenting for each supported device which of the three driver classes it uses and its test coverage.
Excellent AMD GPU support (amdgpu kernel driver + RADV/RadeonSI userspace) on the selected AMD desktop and AMD laptop reference hardware.
Excellent Intel GPU support (i915/xe kernel driver + ANV/Iris userspace) on the selected Intel laptop reference hardware.
ADR: NVIDIA support approach — open drivers (nouveau/NVK/nova) vs proprietary kernel module compatibility vs deferring NVIDIA to post-1.0.
NVIDIA GPU support delivered per the ADR decision, with documented supported generations.
Hardware support on the published reference hardware list (cross-ref §62).
Do not break hardware support unnecessarily.
Power management: CPU frequency scaling, idle states, display power.
Suspend/resume working on the reference laptops.
Bluetooth (audio, input, file transfer) with pairing UI.
Laptop support: lid events, keyboard backlight, touchpad gestures, thermal management, brightness.
Battery reporting, charge thresholds and power-profile policy.
Reliable suspend (s2idle/S3) and resume on reference laptops with measured resume latency.
Select one AMD desktop reference configuration (CPU, GPU, motherboard, NIC, Wi-Fi, audio).
Select one Intel laptop reference configuration.
Select one AMD laptop reference configuration.
Do not promise universal PC compatibility before 1.0; publish an explicit supported-hardware list and treat other hardware as unsupported.
Linux-derived kernel: hardware abstraction layer bridging native Device objects to inherited drivers.
Drivers layer: inherited Linux drivers retained and functioning.
